analogy.p: Imagine the Sun gives the first runner (the producer) a big bag of coins. At each handover, the runner pays out some coins as running costs (respiration/heat), drops some on the track (waste and uneaten parts), and passes only a small bag to the next runner. By the fourth runner there is hardly anything left, so the team cannot have many runners. It breaks down because in a real food chain the coins (energy) cannot be reused, while materials like carbon are recycled by decomposers.

bullets: Example: **lettuce → slug → thrush → sparrowhawk**. The slug eats the lettuce, the thrush eats the slug, and so on.
The arrow points from the organism being eaten to the organism that eats it; it does **not** mean 'eats'.
The source of energy for almost all food chains is the **Sun**, captured by producers in photosynthesis.
A food chain traces the flow of **energy and biomass** (the mass of living material), not the flow of the animals themselves.
The organisms in a food chain are all part of one **community** living in the same habitat.
A **stable community** is one in which all the species and environmental factors are in balance, so that population sizes remain fairly constant over time.
core.p: A **food chain** is a simple diagram showing the feeding relationships in a community: who eats what. It shows how **energy and biomass** are transferred from one organism to the next, and every food chain begins with a **producer**. Each arrow means 'is eaten by' and points in the direction the energy goes, from the food towards the feeder. Food chains are simplifications, because most animals eat more than one thing, but they are the basic building block for understanding ecosystems.

bullets: Producers **synthesise molecules** (glucose, and then starch, cellulose, proteins, lipids) using carbon dioxide, water and light energy.
Some of the glucose is used for **respiration** to release energy for the plant; the rest is used to make biomass, which is available to the next level when eaten.
Examples: grass, oak trees, seaweed, phytoplankton (microscopic algae in water).
Producers occupy **trophic level 1**.
Without producers, there would be no way to bring light energy into the food chain, so every food chain would collapse.
Link to other topics: photosynthesis in Topic 4.4 and the carbon cycle.
core.p: A **producer** is an organism that makes its own food (glucose) from simple inorganic substances using energy from light, by **photosynthesis**. Producers are nearly always green plants or algae, and they are always the first organism in a food chain. They are the entry point of energy into living communities: all the other organisms depend directly or indirectly on the biomass the producers build.

bullets: **Primary consumer:** eats producers (a herbivore). Examples: slug, rabbit, caterpillar.
**Secondary consumer:** eats primary consumers (a carnivore). Example: thrush eating the slug.
**Tertiary consumer:** eats secondary consumers. Example: sparrowhawk eating the thrush.
An **herbivore** eats only plants; a **carnivore** eats only animals; an **omnivore** eats both, so can be at different levels in different food chains.
An **apex predator** is a carnivore at the top of a food chain with **no predators** of its own (for example the lion or killer whale).
The extra consumers beyond tertiary are called quaternary consumers.
core.p: A **consumer** is an organism that cannot make its own food and so eats other organisms. Consumers are named by their position in the chain: **primary consumers** eat producers, **secondary consumers** eat primary consumers, and **tertiary consumers** eat secondary consumers. Because consumers get their energy from eating, they are also called heterotrophs.

bullets: **Predator:** a consumer that kills and eats other animals.
**Prey:** an animal that is killed and eaten by a predator.
A predator may be prey for a bigger predator, so one animal can be both.
Predators regulate prey numbers, preventing the prey population from growing out of control and using up all the producers.
Prey have **adaptations** (camouflage, speed, warning colours) to avoid being eaten; predators have adaptations to catch prey (claws, sharp teeth, good vision).
This is a biotic relationship: **predation** is one of the biotic factors that affect a community.
core.p: Consumers that kill and eat other animals are called **predators**, and the animals they eat are called **prey**. An animal can be both: the thrush is a predator of slugs but prey for the sparrowhawk. The words describe the relationship between two organisms, not a fixed type of animal.

bullets: **Level 1:** producers (lettuce).
**Level 2:** primary consumers (slug).
**Level 3:** secondary consumers (thrush).
**Level 4:** tertiary consumers (sparrowhawk), which are the apex predators in this chain.
Trophic level = the position in the chain, so the number of the consumer type is one less than the level number (secondary consumer = level 3).
An omnivore can be at **more than one trophic level**, depending on what it is eating.
Decomposers are not given a numbered level in the chain but act on all levels.
core.p: A **trophic level** is the feeding level of an organism in a food chain, and levels are numbered starting from 1 at the producers. Every time energy is passed on to the next feeder, the number goes up by one. You are expected to be able to name the trophic level of an organism when given a food chain or web, and to say whether an organism is a producer, primary, secondary or tertiary consumer.

bullets: Decomposers break down **dead organisms** (carcasses, dead leaves) and **waste** (faeces, urine).
They release **mineral ions** (nitrates, phosphates) into the soil, which plants absorb for growth.
They release **carbon dioxide** by respiration, which is used by plants in photosynthesis.
In a stable community, **materials are recycled** (the same atoms are used over and over), but **energy is not**: it is lost as heat and new energy has to enter from the Sun.
Link to other topics: the **carbon cycle** and **decomposition** (the required practical on decay) in Topic 4.7.
Without decomposers dead material would build up and the nutrients would stay locked in it.
core.p: **Decomposers** are microorganisms, mainly **bacteria and fungi**, that break down dead plants and animals and the waste of living organisms. They feed by secreting enzymes onto the dead material and absorbing the soluble products, which releases mineral ions and carbon dioxide back into the environment. This recycling keeps a stable community going, because the materials that producers need are returned to the soil and air.

bullets: In a food web, the arrows still go from the food towards the feeder.
**Interdependence:** each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination or seed dispersal, so changes ripple through the community.
If a **producer** declines, all of the consumers above it have less food, so their populations fall.
If a **predator** is removed, its prey population may increase because fewer are eaten, which may then eat more of its own food.
If a **prey** species declines, the predators will have less food and also decline, unless they switch to another food.
A food web with **many links** is more stable because there are alternative food sources.
Answers should explain the chain of effects step by step, using the words 'so' and 'because'.
core.p: Real communities have many overlapping food chains linked together as a **food web**. A food web shows that most organisms eat several different foods and are eaten by several different predators. Because the species are linked, a change in the population of one species can affect many others: this is called **interdependence**. This is a common exam theme: you may be asked to predict the effect of removing or adding a species.

bullets: Prey peak first, predator peak a little **later** (time lag), because it takes time for the predators to breed.
Prey numbers are always higher than predator numbers, because energy is lost at each level.
Cycle: more prey → more predators → fewer prey → fewer predators → more prey.
Data questions: read the peaks and troughs, and use numbers and the time period.
Other factors, such as disease, weather and food supply, also affect populations, so real cycles are not perfect.
The idea applies to a **stable community** where nothing else changes.
core.p: In a stable community, the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in **cycles**. When there is plenty of prey, the predators have lots of food and breed, so the predator population increases. The extra predators eat more prey, so the prey population falls. With less food, the predators starve or breed less, so the predator population falls. With fewer predators, prey survive and the prey population rises again. On a graph the predator peak comes **after** the prey peak, and the predator curve is smaller.

bullets: Trophic level 1 (producers) is the widest bar at the bottom, and each level above is drawn narrower.
Biomass is usually measured as **dry mass** per area (for example kg per m2), because water content varies.
Drawing: choose a scale, draw each bar centred on the same vertical line, and label each bar with the organism and trophic level.
The pyramid shape shows that **biomass decreases** at each level up the food chain.
A pyramid of numbers can be a strange shape (for example one tree supporting thousands of insects), but a pyramid of biomass is not.
This explains why food chains are rarely longer than four or five levels: too little energy is left to support another level.
Higher/triple content: calculating the percentage efficiency of biomass transfer is covered in the separate note on biomass transfers.
core.p: The amount of living material at each trophic level can be shown in a **pyramid of biomass**. Each bar is drawn to scale, with the producers at the bottom. A pyramid of biomass is nearly always the shape of a pyramid because less biomass is present at each higher level. It is better than a pyramid of numbers because it takes into account the size of organisms: one oak tree is one organism but has a huge mass.

bullets: Not all of an organism is eaten: some parts such as **bones, roots, shells and hair** are not eaten.
Not all of what is eaten is digested: some is egested as **faeces**.
Some absorbed substances are lost in **waste** such as **urine** (urea) and carbon dioxide.

A large amount of glucose is used in **respiration** to release energy for movement, keeping warm (in birds and mammals) and other life processes; this energy is transferred to the surroundings as **heat**.
So the biomass available to the next level is much less, which is why there are fewer organisms at the top.
Warm-blooded animals lose more energy as heat than cold-blooded animals, so they need more food.
The lost energy cannot be reused by the food chain, which is why **energy has to keep coming from the Sun**.
core.h: Why biomass is lost between trophic levels
core.p: Only a small part of the biomass in one level ends up as new biomass in the next. This is the reason the pyramid gets narrower and the chains are short. The losses happen in several ways. Not all of the organism is eaten, not all of what is eaten is absorbed, and a lot of the absorbed material is used to release energy by respiration, which is lost to the surroundings as heat.

bullets: **Shorter food chains** lose less biomass overall, so more of the original energy reaches humans.
**Pesticides** can kill insects that are food for other animals, which then decline (interdependence).
**Removing a top predator** can lead to a rise in its prey and a fall in the producers that they eat.
**Introducing a non-native species** may out-compete native species or eat them.
Conservation programmes use food web knowledge to protect key species.
Link to other topics: **biodiversity**, **farming techniques (triple)**, **carbon cycle**, and **photosynthesis**.
core.h: Applying the ideas: farming and human impacts
core.p: Understanding food chains helps explain how humans can increase food production and what happens when human actions change communities. Because so much is lost between levels, eating plants directly is a more efficient use of land than feeding crops to animals and eating the animals. Shorter food chains waste less energy. Humans can also disrupt food webs by pollution, pesticides and over-hunting.

exam: Always **start a food chain with a producer** and draw arrows from the food towards the feeder.
For 'name the trophic level' give the number and the word: 'trophic level 3, secondary consumer'.
Use the **exact terms**: producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, tertiary consumer, apex predator, decomposer.
For 'what happens to X if Y decreases' (3 to 4 marks) give a chain of reasoning: fewer Y, so less food for X, so X decreases; and say what happens to the things X eats.
Mention **'interdependence'** in answers about food webs.
For **predator-prey graphs**, use values and times, and say that the predator peak follows the prey peak.
For 'why does biomass decrease along a food chain?' (3 or 4 marks) give at least three reasons: respiration (heat), egestion, excretion and parts not eaten.
Do not write 'energy is used up'; write 'lost as heat to the surroundings'.
To draw a **pyramid of biomass**, choose a scale, draw bars centred, and label each level.
For 6 mark questions, link together producers, energy from the Sun, biomass transfer, losses and the effect on numbers.
Percentage calculations: (biomass in the higher level / biomass in the lower level) x 100, with units cancelled.
Look at the number of marks: 1 mark is a single fact, 2 marks need a reason, 4 and 6 marks need linked ideas.

mistakes.r: The arrow shows the direction of energy transfer, from the organism eaten to the one that eats it.
The producer is the green plant or alga that makes food by photosynthesis; the Sun is the source of energy.
Energy is lost to the surroundings as heat from respiration, in waste and in uneaten parts. Energy is transferred, not destroyed.
mistakes.w: Energy is 'used up' or 'destroyed' between levels.

mistakes.r: Secondary consumers are at trophic level 3, because producers are level 1.
mistakes.w: Secondary consumers are at trophic level 2.

mistakes.r: The prey numbers will increase because fewer are eaten, which may then reduce the producers they eat.
mistakes.w: If the predator is removed, the prey will stay the same.

mistakes.r: Biomass is lost through respiration, egestion, excretion and parts not eaten.
mistakes.w: Biomass is lost because animals do not eat enough.

mistakes.r: Decomposers recycle materials from dead organisms and waste back into the soil and air, so producers can use them.
mistakes.w: Decomposers are not part of the food chain.

mistakes.r: A pyramid of biomass shows the mass of living material at each level, drawn to scale.
mistakes.w: Pyramid of biomass is the same as a pyramid of numbers.

mistakes.r: The predator peak comes after the prey peak, with a time lag.
mistakes.w: Predator numbers peak at the same time as prey.

summary: You need to be able to describe feeding relationships using food chains and food webs, name producers, primary, secondary and tertiary consumers, predators and prey, and number trophic levels starting at 1 for producers. You also need to understand pyramids of biomass, why biomass decreases up a chain, and how a change in one population affects others.

terms.d: A diagram showing the feeding relationships between organisms, starting with a producer, with arrows showing the direction of energy flow.
A diagram of several linked food chains in a community.
An organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis; usually a green plant or alga.
An organism that gets its energy by eating other organisms.
A consumer that eats primary consumers.
A consumer that eats secondary consumers.
A carnivore at the top of a food chain with no predators.
A consumer that kills and eats other animals.
An animal that is killed and eaten by a predator.
The position of an organism in a food chain, numbered from 1 at the producers.
A microorganism (bacterium or fungus) that breaks down dead organisms and waste, returning nutrients to the environment.
The mass of living material (usually dry mass) in organisms.
A diagram showing the biomass at each trophic level of a food chain, drawn to scale.
The way species in a community depend on each other, so that changes in one affect others.
A community in which all species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.
An animal that eats only plants.
An animal that eats only other animals.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.

worked.q: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk. (a) Name the producer. (b) What trophic level is the frog? (c) Name the apex predator. (3 marks)
steps: The producer is the first in the chain and makes food by photosynthesis: grass.
Grass is level 1, grasshopper level 2, frog level 3.
The hawk is at the top and has no predators.

worked.ans: Frogs decrease because less food; grass increases because fewer grasshoppers eat it; snakes also decrease, because the species are interdependent.
worked.q: A pesticide kills most of the grasshoppers. Explain the effect on the numbers of frogs and on the grass. (4 marks)
steps: The grasshoppers are the food of the frogs, so frogs have less food and their numbers decrease (they starve or breed less).
The grasshoppers no longer eat the grass, so the grass population increases.
The decrease in frogs will in turn cause a decrease in the snakes, because of interdependence.

worked.ans: 7.5%; lost through respiration (heat), waste (faeces/urine) and uneaten parts
worked.q: The biomass of rabbits in a field is 800 kg and the biomass of the foxes that eat them is 60 kg. Calculate the percentage of biomass passed on and give two reasons it is not 100%. (4 marks)
steps: Reasons: some biomass is lost as heat from respiration; some is lost in faeces and urine; some parts (bones, fur) are not eaten.
